blocks.text: Commercial property behaves differently from houses, so the headline price indexes do not help much. This page puts two published data sets side by side for the Fraser Valley: what commercial property actually sold for in the second quarter of 2026, and how much industrial space is empty, what it asks, and what is being built in the third quarter.
Commercial sales in the Lower Mainland, Q2 2026

The Lower Mainland recorded 285 commercial sales worth $1.54 billion in the second quarter of 2026. The number of sales was 2.7% lower than a year earlier and 14.2% lower than the first quarter, while dollar volume was up 16.3% from a year earlier. Fewer deals, but bigger ones on average.

blocks.text: Two classes moved against the trend. Office sales fell to 46 from 64 a year earlier, yet office dollar volume was up 68.4% because the year-earlier quarter was so small. Industrial held steady at 81 sales but its dollar volume was down 31.9%, which means the typical industrial deal was smaller.

blocks.text: These nine municipalities made up 125 of the region's 285 commercial sales, or 44%. Surrey led with 53 sales (up from 44) and $249.9M in volume, and $147.5M of that was land. Half of Langley's 20 sales were retail or other (10), the highest share among the nine.

Treat the dollar figures for the smaller areas with care. Chilliwack's 13 sales added up to $27.4M, against $165.6M from 10 sales a year earlier. With counts this low, one large sale moves the total, so the number of sales says more than the dollars do.
Industrial space: vacancy, rents and new supply, Q3 2026

Across the 14 submarkets Avison Young tracks, from Vancouver out to Chilliwack, 4.0% of industrial space was vacant in the third quarter and 4.9% was available, down from 5.4% available in the second quarter. Average asking net rent was $19.40 per square foot, with another $7.27 on average in additional rent. About 3.56 million square feet was under construction in 31 projects, and 61% of that space was already pre-committed.

blocks.text: The spread inside the Fraser Valley is wide. Chilliwack was the tightest at 0.9% vacant, while Maple Ridge / Pitt Meadows was the loosest at 7.9%. Asking net rent ran from $15.37 in Chilliwack to $19.66 in Surrey, a gap of $4.29 a square foot between the cheapest and the dearest of these markets.

Supply is the other story. Surrey has 1,628,917 square feet under construction, 46% of the whole Metro pipeline, even though its net absorption for the quarter was −220,336 square feet, meaning more space was given back than taken up. Delta went the other way: 420,243 square feet of net absorption and 3.4% vacancy. Langley's net absorption was −75,016 square feet and its vacancy 5.7%.
What the numbers mean for an owner-user, investor or seller

For an owner-user buying a unit or a building, the sales data says most industrial deals are small. In the Lower Mainland in Q2, 62 of the 81 industrial sales were under $3 million, and the largest group, 34, sat between $1 million and $2 million. In Chilliwack, where vacancy was 0.9%, expect few comparable choices, and sales that depend on what happens to come up.

For an investor, the gap between net rent and additional rent matters as much as the headline. In the Fraser Valley markets above, additional rent adds between $5.20 and $6.95 to the asking rent, so two buildings with the same net rent can cost a tenant very different amounts.

For an owner thinking about selling, land was the largest dollar class in the quarter: 56 sales for $536.6 million, up 38.9% from a year earlier. The count has stayed between 50 and 56 sales for five straight quarters, so activity has been steady. A site that could be redeveloped is a different sale from a building valued on its rent.
How to read these two reports together

They measure different things in different places. The GVR figures count completed sales registered with the Land Title and Survey Authority of BC, and they exclude share sales. Avison Young's figures describe leasing space and are grouped by submarket, so Maple Ridge and Pitt Meadows appear together and Tsawwassen means the Tsawwassen First Nation lands. A city that is quiet in one report can still be busy in the other.
Neither report describes your own building. Zoning, lot size, ceiling height, loading, and whether the space is strata or freehold change value more than the submarket average does.

faq.q: What is the difference between vacancy and availability in the industrial table?
faq.a: Both are published by Avison Young and availability is the larger number because it counts more space than just the empty space. In Surrey, for example, 1,872,998 square feet was vacant while 2,100,222 square feet was available. Availability usually also includes space that is being marketed but not yet empty, such as a tenant's space that is coming up.

faq.q: Why do the sales report and the rent report show different areas?
faq.a: They are produced by different organizations for different purposes. GVR's Commercial Edge counts registered sales by municipality. Avison Young reports leasing space by submarket and combines Maple Ridge with Pitt Meadows.

faq.q: Does the sales data include commercial listings that are for sale now?
faq.a: No. It counts completed sales registered at the Land Title and Survey Authority of BC. Current listings are on the commercial search page.
GVR publishes Commercial Edge quarterly with a lag of about three months, and Avison Young publishes its industrial report each quarter. I update this page when each new report is out.
